red.focus: Break an obligation into facts the law must establish
red.summary: Legal duties are tested through explicit rules and evidence. Learn to identify what a person must do, why, and what event might constitute noncompliance.
checklist: I can state a duty in plain language
I can identify the person obligated
I can separate duty from breach and consequence

sections.title: One Sentence Can Clarify the Issue
sections.body_md: A signed contract says a supplier must deliver equipment by Friday. That gives a concrete duty to identify and compare with what happened. If the goods arrive Monday, there may be a breach—but the legal result depends on interpretation, excuses, remedies and the governing law. A legal beginner should not jump from late delivery to a dramatic conclusion. State the promise, the relevant date, the actual conduct, and the rule supplying legal force.

sections.title: Duty Is Not the Same as Harm
sections.body_md: A traffic rule may require a motorist to stop at a red light even if nobody is injured when they fail to stop. In a private damages claim, however, actual injury and causation may be additional elements. This is why an element chart matters: duty, breach, harm and legal consequence should not be collapsed. Different causes of action require different elements, and some do not use all these terms. The first analytic question is always what this specific rule requires.

sections.title: Find the Actor and the Source
sections.body_md: A company's duty may arise from statute, contract, fiduciary relationship or a recognized tort principle. An employee's personal obligation may be different from the organization's. For each duty ask: who is bound, to whom or for whose protection, what conduct is required, and what source imposes it? The question becomes much easier to solve once these are written explicitly. That discipline prevents legal argument from depending on vague assertions that someone should have behaved better.

yellow.summary: Develop the discipline of linking each required condition of a claim to supporting and adverse evidence. Learn why proving some elements does not prove the whole case.
checklist: I can construct a legal elements matrix
I can identify unknown facts relevant to each element
I can separate a defense from denial of an element

sections.title: A Claim Is a Set of Conditions
sections.body_md: Suppose a claimant alleges negligent injury. The applicable legal order may require a duty of care, breach, causation, legally recognized damage and consideration of defenses. These words are not identical in every system. Write each required condition separately, then list evidence supporting, opposing or missing for it. If a necessary element is not shown under the governing standard, the claim may fail even if other elements are strong. This prevents selective reasoning based on sympathy or narrative force.

sections.title: Facts Must Do Analytical Work
sections.body_md: A witness says the floor was wet. That may support a breach question, but does not alone prove how long the spill existed or whether the defendant had the legally required opportunity to respond. A record showing maintenance inspections may matter differently. Good reasoning ties each fact to an element and explains its significance. Extraneous detail should be removed unless it changes a rule's application. This is how a concise analysis can be more rigorous than a long retelling.

sections.title: Defenses and Burdens Are Separate
sections.body_md: A defendant may deny that a duty existed or assert that a special defense applies despite the claimant's evidence. The allocation of burdens can differ. The writer must label a response accurately: an element denial attacks what the claimant must establish; an affirmative defense introduces a legally recognized additional issue. A clear matrix should show whose burden applies where, with any uncertainty disclosed. This structure makes later drafting and oral argument far easier.

orange.focus: Analyze duties involving multiple actors and institutions
orange.summary: Learn to avoid assigning responsibility to the most visible person when law distributes duties among organizations, officials and individuals. Separate obligations from causal roles and legal powers.
checklist: I can identify multiple potential duty holders
I can distinguish personal and institutional obligations
I can assess attribution and available defenses

sections.title: The Visible Actor May Not Be the Only One
sections.body_md: A hospital patient is harmed after a record is misplaced, a medication order is unclear, and staffing protocols are inadequate. Different persons may have distinct duties under professional rules, employment law and the institution's obligations. A lawyer should not assume that the last person touching the record caused or legally answers for everything. Draw a duty map showing each actor, source, required conduct and relationship to the injury. Then analyze causation and defenses separately.

sections.title: Organizations Act Through People
sections.body_md: An entity can be responsible for conduct of employees or agents under recognized attribution rules. These rules differ by jurisdiction and claim. Personal wrongdoing, vicarious liability, regulatory responsibility and direct organizational fault are not synonyms. Advanced analysis identifies which theory permits liability against which defendant, and what additional facts each theory requires. This prevents both overcharging individuals and allowing institutions to disappear behind formal organizational charts.

sections.title: When Duties Conflict
sections.body_md: A professional may face confidentiality obligations and a statutory reporting requirement triggered by particular facts. The correct response depends on the governing hierarchy, statutory conditions and any recognized exceptions. Ethical alarm is not a substitute for legal analysis. Identify each duty's source, scope, trigger and consequence; then determine whether the apparent conflict can be reconciled. If the law remains uncertain, the client deserves an explanation of the competing risks and permitted choices.

black.focus: Critique duties and institutional accountability through precise legal reasoning
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate whether a doctrine distributes obligations fairly among persons who control risks and persons who bear them. Distinguish legal interpretation from proposals for institutional reform.
checklist: I can evaluate a legal duty's normative justification
I can critique overbroad or underinclusive attribution
I can design duty rules sensitive to vulnerability and administrability

sections.title: Why Does This Duty Exist?
sections.body_md: A doctrine might impose responsibility because an actor controls a risk, made a promise, induced reliance, or occupies a position of trust. These explanations are not interchangeable. A doctoral lawyer must identify which rationale underlies the applicable law and whether the proposed interpretation fits its limits. If an expanding duty would protect victims but create indefinite responsibility, that cost must be confronted openly. A legal conclusion is strongest when its normative reasoning remains consistent with institutional authority.

sections.title: Duties Can Track Power Poorly
sections.body_md: A delivery worker may face direct liability for an incident shaped by platform instructions and time pressure beyond their control. The governing doctrine may or may not assign responsibility to the platform. The analyst should map actual control, foreseeability, contractual arrangements and public protections, then separate the current law from suggested reform. A theory that overlooks structural vulnerability can be formally neat and practically unjust. Conversely, blaming all powerful institutions for all outcomes neglects causal and legal boundaries.

sections.title: Serve Through Candor
sections.body_md: In a difficult case, the client may seek a categorical answer about who should pay. Ethical excellence requires explaining the difference between moral responsibility, legal duty and provable liability. An opinion should tell the client what can be established, what remains uncertain, and where a law reform argument would begin. The legal scholar's task is not to transform every tragedy into an effortless lawsuit; it is to make law both intelligible and responsive to those whose lives it governs.
